claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE checkpoints as many frames as possible without waiting for readers or writers to finish.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE Checkpoint as many frames as possible without waiting for any database readers or writers to finish

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE never invokes the busy-handler callback.
claims.quote: The busy-handler callback is never invoked in the SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE mode. On the other hand, passive mode might leave the checkpoint unfinished

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL waits until there is no writer and all readers use the most recent database snapshot.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL This mode blocks (it invokes the busy-handler callback ) until there is no database writer and all readers are reading from the most recent database snapshot.

claims.text: While SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL is pending, it blocks new writers but permits new readers.
claims.quote: This mode blocks new database writers while it is pending, but new database readers are allowed to continue unimpeded.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART additionally waits after checkpointing until all readers read only from the database file.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART This mode works the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL with the addition that after checkpointing the log file it blocks (calls the busy-handler callback ) until all readers are reading from the database file only.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE adds truncation to zero bytes immediately before a successful return to the behavior of SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE This mode works the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART with the addition that it also truncates the log file to zero bytes just prior to a successful return.

claims.text: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_NOOP checkpoints zero frames and exists to retrieve the pnLog and pnCkpt output values.
claims.quote: SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_NOOP This mode always checkpoints zero frames. The only reason to invoke a NOOP checkpoint is to access the values returned by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() via output parameters *pnLog and *pnCkpt.

claims.text: If overlapping readers always leave at least one reader active, checkpoints cannot complete and the WAL grows without bound.
claims.quote: if a database has many concurrent overlapping readers and there is always at least one active reader, then no checkpoints will be able to complete and hence the WAL file will grow without bound.

claims.text: Checkpoint starvation can be avoided by attempting checkpoints during reader gaps when no processes are reading.
claims.quote: This scenario can be avoided by ensuring that there are "reader gaps": times when no processes are reading from the database and that checkpoints are attempted during those times.

claims.text: sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint(D,N) triggers automatic checkpointing after a commit if the WAL contains at least N frames.
claims.quote: causes any database on database connection D to automatically checkpoint after committing a transaction if there are N or more frames in the write-ahead log file.

claims.text: Passing N equal to zero or a negative value disables automatic checkpoints.
claims.quote: Passing zero or a negative value as the N parameter disables automatic checkpoints entirely.

claims.text: Registering a sqlite3_wal_hook() callback disables automatic checkpointing configured by sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint().
claims.quote: Likewise, registering a callback using sqlite3_wal_hook() disables the automatic checkpoint mechanism configured by this function.

claims.text: By default, the thread performing the COMMIT that crosses the WAL size limit also runs the checkpoint.
claims.quote: By default, the checkpoint will be run automatically by the same thread that does the COMMIT that pushes the WAL over its size limit.

claims.text: Maximizing read performance favors keeping the WAL small through frequent checkpoints.
claims.quote: To maximize the read performance, one wants to keep the WAL as small as possible and hence run checkpoints frequently, perhaps as often as every COMMIT.

claims.text: If another process holds the checkpoint lock, the checkpoint returns SQLITE_BUSY without invoking the configured busy handler.
claims.quote: If any other process is running a checkpoint operation at the same time, the lock cannot be obtained and SQLITE_BUSY is returned. Even if there is a busy-handler configured, it will not be invoked

claims.text: If the busy handler returns zero before obtaining the writer lock or while waiting for readers, checkpointing continues with PASSIVE behavior.
claims.quote: If the busy-handler returns 0 before the writer lock is obtained or while waiting for database readers, the checkpoint operation proceeds from that point in the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE

claims.text: Checkpointing normally reuses the WAL from its beginning rather than truncating it, except when journal_size_limit is set.
claims.quote: The checkpoint does not normally truncate the WAL file (unless the journal_size_limit pragma is set). Instead, it merely causes SQLite to start overwriting the WAL file from the beginning.

claims.text: A writer rewinds the WAL when its contents have been transferred and synced and no readers use the WAL.
claims.quote: if the entire WAL has been transferred into the database and synced and if no readers are making use of the WAL, then the writer will rewind the WAL back to the beginning

claims.text: The WAL must reach persistent storage before checkpointing moves its content into the database.
claims.quote: The WAL must be synced to persistent storage prior to moving content from the WAL into the database

claims.text: Writers sync the WAL at every commit with PRAGMA synchronous=FULL but omit that sync with PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL.
claims.quote: Writers sync the WAL on every transaction commit if PRAGMA synchronous is set to FULL but omit this sync if PRAGMA synchronous is set to NORMAL.

claims.text: With PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL, checkpointing is the only operation that issues an I/O barrier or sync.
claims.quote: Note that with PRAGMA synchronous set to NORMAL, the checkpoint is the only operation to issue an I/O barrier or sync operation

claims.text: The last connection to close performs a final checkpoint and deletes the WAL and associated shared-memory file.
claims.quote: When the last connection to a database closes, that connection does one last checkpoint and then deletes the WAL and its associated shared-memory file, to clean up the disk.

claims.text: pnCkpt reports the total checkpointed frames in the log, including frames checkpointed before the current call.
claims.quote: *pnCkpt is set to the total number of checkpointed frames in the log file (including any that were already checkpointed before the function was called)

claims.text: After a successful SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE, both pnLog and pnCkpt are zero.
claims.quote: upon successful completion of an SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE, the log file will have been truncated to zero bytes and so both *pnLog and *pnCkpt will be set to zero.

claims.text: A reader's end mark remains fixed for its transaction, giving that transaction a single point-in-time view.
claims.quote: for any particular reader, the end mark is unchanged for the duration of the transaction, thus ensuring that a single read transaction only sees the database content as it existed at a single point in time.

claims.text: A checkpoint must stop when it reaches a WAL page beyond any current reader's end mark.
claims.quote: A checkpoint can run concurrently with readers, however the checkpoint must stop when it reaches a page in the WAL that is past the end mark of any current reader.

claims.text: SQLite permits only one WAL writer at a time because there is only one WAL file.
claims.quote: However, since there is only one WAL file, there can only be one writer at a time.

claims.text: If zDb is NULL or an empty string, checkpointing is attempted on every attached WAL database.
claims.quote: If parameter zDb is NULL or points to a zero length string, then the specified operation is attempted on all WAL databases attached to database connection db.

claims.text: When targeting all attached WAL databases, SQLITE_BUSY from one database does not prevent attempts on the remaining databases.
claims.quote: If an SQLITE_BUSY error is encountered when processing one or more of the attached WAL databases, the operation is still attempted on any remaining attached databases and SQLITE_BUSY is returned at the end.

claims.text: The WAL cannot be reset during a write transaction because checkpoint completion requires other transactions to have stopped.
claims.quote: A checkpoint can only complete when no other transactions are running, which means the WAL file cannot be reset in the middle of a write transaction.

claims.text: The shared-memory wal-index helps readers locate WAL pages quickly with minimal I/O.
claims.quote: a data structure called the "wal-index" is maintained in shared memory which helps readers locate pages in the WAL quickly and with a minimum of I/O.

claims.text: The wal-index shared-memory requirement confines readers to one machine and prevents this WAL implementation from working on a network filesystem.
claims.quote: the use of shared memory means that all readers must exist on the same machine. This is why the write-ahead log implementation will not work on a network filesystem.

claims.text: After a crash or ROLLBACK, rollback-journal recovery restores original database content from the journal.
claims.quote: In the event of a crash or ROLLBACK , the original content contained in the rollback journal is played back into the database file to revert the database file to its original state.

claims.text: The database file must be synced before the WAL is reset.
claims.quote: and the database file must be synced prior to resetting the WAL. Checkpoint also requires more seeking.
